ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) in pregnancy is a clot in a deep vein or the lungs, driven by a hypercoagulable state and immobility. Early recognition and anticoagulation save lives.

sections.p: VTE is a clot in a deep vein (usually lower limb) or pulmonary artery. Diagnosis combines clinical suspicion with imaging and laboratory tests.
b: Clinical signs: unilateral leg pain, swelling, warmth; sudden dyspnea, chest pain

t.b: Detects thrombus in leg veins; positive confirms DVT
Visualises embolus in pulmonary arteries; positive confirms PE
Elevated in VTE; low levels rule out in low‑risk patients; may be falsely high in pregnancy

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ involvement and haemodynamic stability.
b: Class I: isolated DVT, stable haemodynamics
Class II: PE with stable haemodynamics
Class III: massive PE, haemodynamic instability

sections.p: Pregnancy itself is a major risk factor due to hormonal changes and venous stasis. Other common causes in low‑resource settings include infections and herbal remedies.
Symptoms vary with location; DVT presents with leg pain and swelling, PE with sudden shortness of breath and chest pain.
b: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia

sections.p: Use a stepwise approach, prioritising tests that are available.

t.b: Rule in/out DVT; normal in low‑risk patients
Confirm PE; consider if haemodynamically stable
Gold standard when CT is unavailable; invasive
Assess for inherited or acquired thrombophilia

sections.p: Urgent signs include haemodynamic collapse, massive haemoptysis, or sudden severe leg swelling.
Treat the underlying cause, provide anticoagulation, and monitor for bleeding.
b: Anticoagulation with low‑molecular‑weight heparin; switch to warfarin or DOACs when stable

t.b: Preferred in pregnancy; reduces recurrence; avoid unfractionated heparin unless rapid reversal needed
Used postpartum; avoid in pregnancy due to teratogenicity

sections.p: Long‑term anticoagulation depends on recurrence risk. Prevention focuses on early mobilisation and mechanical prophylaxis.

faq.a: Yes, pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state that increases VTE risk.

faq.q: What is the safest anticoagulant in pregnancy?
faq.a: Low‑molecular‑weight heparin is preferred; warfarin is avoided.

faq.q: How long should anticoagulation continue after a first VTE?
faq.a: Typically 3–6 months, longer if ongoing risk factors exist.
